texts: mixed: the three hunts, the cove and the dates all land, but two things are off - three date phrases stacked on one clause have no licensed shape, so the parse had to invent one hunt per date on its own authority, and the hunting is recorded only of the pack, never handed down to the individual sky-cats. Splitting the dates fixes the first and keeps one pack for the later 'the sky-cats' reference: 'Sky-cats hunted at the Sunken Cove on day 667 of Year 2. The sky-cats hunted at the Sunken Cove on day 668 of Year 2. The sky-cats hunted at the Sunken Cove on day 669 of Year 2.'

bad: 'asked ... for permission' is parsed as if the permission were the direct object of the asking, and the link from the permission to the burning is given the wrong preposition, so 'what did he ask the Council for?' will not resolve. Say it with clauses instead of the noun 'permission': 'On day 670 of Year 2, Bevin Coombe asked the Council to let him burn wintergloss at the Stilllight Lantern for one night.' That still leaves the proposed burning as its own not-yet-happened event, which the later 'the test' sentences point back at.
good. 'the test' is resolved to the burning Bevin Coombe proposed, and that same referent carries through to the Council's record at the end of the passage.
good. the agent, the wintergloss, the lantern as destination and the sundown timing are all carried.
good. the lantern is what burns, the wintergloss is what is burned, and 'alongside mire-essence' is kept as the phrase you wrote rather than folded into some other relation.
good. short and fully covered, with mist-light recorded as a kind of light.
good. the wintergloss is what repels, the nightmoths are what is repelled, and the lantern is what they are driven away from.
good. the count of three rides on the moths, and 'that night' correctly picks up day 670 of Year 2 from earlier in the passage.

bad: two things are lost. 'About twelve' has no licensed form - the count slot takes a whole number, so the parse forced a fuzzy value into it, and the compliant alternative would drop the twelve altogether; and 'on a normal night' has to become a one-off night object, which then fails to line up with the plain 'night' used for 'that night' in the previous sentence. Put the typicality in an adverb and the count in a plain number: 'Twelve nightmoths usually gather at the Stilllight Lantern at night.' If the count must stay approximate, use an explicit bound instead: 'At least ten nightmoths usually gather at the Stilllight Lantern at night.'

mixed: the denial is recorded of the pack as a whole but not of the individual sky-cats, so 'did this sky-cat descend?' comes back unknown instead of no. Use the explicit quantifier, which forces the per-cat denial: 'None of the sky-cats descended into the Sunken Cove that night.'
good. the reporter, the Council as recipient and the reported result are all covered.
good. the recording is tied back to the same test the Council approved, and the test is correctly left unaltered by being recorded.
